newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts up in thin trade as budget blues fade.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts up in thin trade as budget blues fade.

text.p: 1300 GMT - UK gilts were up nearly half a point by the midsession as dealers shook off post-budget blues in thin trading. No key data. * LIFFE September gilts up 12/32 at 114-27/32.
UK government bonds (gilts) were comfortably up by the midsession on Friday on mixed buying into the long end amid thin trading, market players said.
"The market is looking very good...we are tilting down to the long end," said one trader. "Budget blues are still here, but they are in the background."
The buying was both local and foreign although the Independence Day holiday in the U.S. meant there was no interest from that side, the trader said.
"It is relatively thin," the trader said.
The front month September gilt futures contract was up 12/32 on the previous close at 114-27/32 by 1300 GMT, well up on the open of 114-11/32 having clawed back Thursday's after hours losses.

Analysts said that Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget on Wednesday did not go far enough to slow buoyant consumer demand and many fear an interest rate rise is inevitable to halt inflation.
Traders said the market had been discounting up to a 50 basis point rise following the Bank of England monetary policy meeting, who Brown empowered to set rates, next Wednesday and Thursday.
"Rates will not be going up by as much as the market was discounting which is good for gilts, particularly on the short end," the trader said.
"We have had a bit of a rally here this morning, it has been rather thin volume," said another trader.
He added that since lunch there had been little action and many were hoping to follow the U.S. and enjoy a long weekend.
"It is pretty dull waiting for until a quarter past four when they can go home," he said.
At the short end of the yield curve, LIFFE September short sterling was unchanged from its two point rise at the open to 92.85, discounting an interest rate rise of half a point.
As for the budget, he said the worries had all but disappeared, the trader said.
"Everyone has forgotten about it," the trader said.
